children: In India, insurance is still sold rather than bought, and for the past three years, the seller has often been paid far more than the service justified. On September 23, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) released a consultation paper titled ‘Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution’, proposing the most sweeping reset of how policies reach customers since it removed product-wise commission caps in 2023.

First, the fragmented universe of corporate agents, brokers, web aggregators, and motor service providers would collapse into three categories, namely Insurance Distribution Entities, Insurance Distribution Persons, and Market Infrastructure Institutions, with lower capital requirements, reduced fees, and the freedom to engage in other financial and non-financial business.

Second, the Expense of Management ceiling for life insurers would become a company-level limit of 15 per cent of gross direct premium within two years and 12.5 per cent within five years, while general insurers would glide from 30 per cent of gross written premium to 20 per cent of gross direct premium. Third, commissions would be capped by segment, channel and product complexity.

Health policies would carry 15-20 per cent on the first sale, and 5-10 per cent on renewal or porting; new vehicle motor cover would pay nothing on the third-party premium and 5 per cent on own damage; and life cover sold with loans would pay just 2 per cent on single-premium policies.

Fourth, conduct rules would tighten, with a ban on compulsory bundling with loans, documented suitability, the seller’s identity linked to every policy, clawback of commission for mis-selling, and no volume-linked incentives for bank and NBFC staff.

Between FY23 and FY25, motor premiums grew 34 per cent, while motor commissions grew 259 per cent; in retail health, premiums rose 53 per cent, against an 118 per cent jump in commissions. Banks with multiple insurer tie-ups paid out an average of 33 per cent of new business premium, rising to 72 per cent in some cases, compared with 13 per cent for single tie-ups.

The reset will redistribute this surplus. Lenders feel it first, since insurance fees make up roughly 16 per cent of pre-provision operating profit at Yes Bank and 12 per cent at IDFC First Bank, and brokerages estimate 3-25 per cent of pre-tax profit for select NBFCs.

Insurers may see weaker bank volumes at first but should gain from lower acquisition costs. IRDAI may cap what insurers pay banks, but staff remuneration within banks falls under the Reserve Bank of India, so sales targets could quietly reappear as general performance bonuses. The principle of ‘same structure, same functions, same norms’ also sits uneasily with a 25 per cent cap for agents, compared with 20 per cent for banks and brokers, when selling the identical long-term plan.

IRDAI need to use the consultation window to close these gaps without diluting its core intent. A joint IRDAI and RBI circular on incentives for bank and NBFC staff would stop arbitrage at its source. Insurers should report how expense savings are passed on, through premium revisions in general insurance and bonus declarations in life insurance. Clawback should be triggered by objective markers such as free-look cancellations, early lapses, and complaints upheld by the Insurance Ombudsman. Rewards for underserved areas should be tied to PIN codes verified through the Public Insurance Registry.

Commission should be disclosed in rupees at the point of sale, not as a percentage buried in a brochure. A clear transition schedule would ease the shock for agents and bank staff whose livelihoods depend on this chain, and a formal review after two years would allow correction based on evidence. If implemented with care, we could expect a shift from insurance sold to insurance bought.

title: Taking stock of IRDAI’s distribution reset
